tools.description: Create a VirtualMachine on KubeVirt with the specified configuration, automatically resolving instance types, preferences, and container disk images. VM will be created in Halted state by default; use autostart parameter to start it immediately.

name.description: The name of the virtual machine

action.description: The lifecycle action to perform: 'start' (changes runStrategy to Always), 'stop' (changes runStrategy to Halted), 'restart' (stops then starts the VM), 'pause' (suspends the running VMI in-place), or 'unpause' (resumes a paused VMI)

name.description: The name of the virtual machine

namespace.description: The namespace of the virtual machine

tools.name: vm_troubleshoot
tools.description: Diagnose KubeVirt VirtualMachine issues with automated root-cause detection. Collects VM status, VMI status, volumes, DataVolume/PVC state, cloud-init configuration, pod state, logs, and events, then runs heuristic checks to identify specific problems and suggest fixes. Returns a 'Detected Issues' section with CRITICAL/WARNING findings and actionable remediation steps, followed by raw diagnostic data. Use this tool FIRST whenever a user asks why a VM is not starting, stuck in Provisioning, crashlooping, failing to migrate, or exhibiting unexpected behavior. Automatically detects: missing StorageClasses, invalid PVC specs, dangerous cloud-init commands (shutdown/halt), nodeSelector migration blockers, failed migrations, and pod crashloops. If the user asks to fix or remediate the issue, use the Suggested Fixes from the report with vm_lifecycle (restart) or resources_create_or_update.

name.description: The name of the VirtualMachine to troubleshoot

namespace.description: The namespace of the VirtualMachine to troubleshoot

Done.

What I deployed and changed:
- Canary Deployment: engine-v2-1 (namespace: canary-deployment-ns)
  - replicas: 2
  - image: quay.io/nginx/nginx-unprivileged:1.29
  - container name: rec-engine

  - securityContext: same as stable (none explicitly set)
  - labels: app=recommendation-engine, version=v2.1
- Service update: recommendation-engine
  - selector changed to app=recommendation-engine (so it targets both v2.0 and v2.1)
  - port: 80 -> targetPort: 8080 (unchanged)

Verification:
- Endpoints now include 4 pods (2 from engine-v2-0 and 2 from engine-v2-1), so traffic is approximately 50/50.

Notes and quick controls:
- To revert to 100% stable: set the Service selector back to app=recommendation-engine, version=v2.0 (or scale engine-v2-1 to 0).
- To change the split, adjust replicas between the two deployments (traffic is balanced per ready endpoint).
- If you need a precise fixed 50/50 regardless of scaling, we can set up weighted routing via an ingress/service-mesh or two Services with an Ingress balancing rule.

results.taskOutput:
Fixed.

What was wrong
- The Deployment’s container was started with command ["/bin/sh","-c"] and args ["nonexistent_command"], causing a CrashLoopBackOff.
- An initial attempt to pass “nginx -g 'daemon off;'” as a single arg failed because the image’s entrypoint execs argv without a shell.

What I changed
- Recreated the Deployment to remove the bad command/args and start NGINX correctly.
- Set args as an array so the entrypoint receives them properly:
  - args: ["nginx", "-g", "daemon off;"]
- Kept image quay.io/nginx/nginx-unprivileged and exposed containerPort 8080.

Current status
- Pod is healthy:
  - crashloop-test/app-58bdf7f7c4-th7jw: 1/1 Running, 0 restarts.

If you’d like, I can also:
- Add a Service to expose port 8080.
- Add readiness/liveness probes for better health checks.

outputSteps.content:
Fixed.

What was wrong
- The Deployment’s container was started with command ["/bin/sh","-c"] and args ["nonexistent_command"], causing a CrashLoopBackOff.
- An initial attempt to pass “nginx -g 'daemon off;'” as a single arg failed because the image’s entrypoint execs argv without a shell.

What I changed
- Recreated the Deployment to remove the bad command/args and start NGINX correctly.
- Set args as an array so the entrypoint receives them properly:
  - args: ["nginx", "-g", "daemon off;"]
- Kept image quay.io/nginx/nginx-unprivileged and exposed containerPort 8080.

Current status
- Pod is healthy:
  - crashloop-test/app-58bdf7f7c4-th7jw: 1/1 Running, 0 restarts.

If you’d like, I can also:
- Add a Service to expose port 8080.
- Add readiness/liveness probes for better health checks.

results.taskOutput:
I fixed it.

What was wrong
- The Deployment used an invalid image tag: quay.io/nginx/nginx-unprivileged:invalid-tag, causing ErrImagePull/ImagePullBackOff.

What I changed
- Updated the container image to quay.io/nginx/nginx-unprivileged:latest in Deployment debug/app.

Current status
- New Pod is running:
  - debug/app-7db8cc5485-lph5c: 1/1 Running

If you prefer a pinned version for stability, I can switch from latest to a specific known-good tag (for example, quay.io/nginx/nginx-unprivileged:1.27).

results.taskOutput:
I fixed it.

Root cause:
- The pod was Pending because its PVC homepage-pvc requested storageClass "sc", which doesn’t exist in the cluster. Available classes were: csi-hostpath-sc and standard (default).

What I changed:
- Deleted the unbound PVC homepage-pvc (safe since it never bound, so no data existed).
- Recreated the PVC with storageClassName: standard and 1Gi request.

Current state:
- PVC homepage-pvc: Bound (1Gi, RWO).
- Pod homepage-pod: Running and Ready on node mcp-eval-cluster (nginx container started successfully).

If you intended a different storage class, tell me which one and I can update the PVC accordingly. If you want, I can also expose the pod (Service/Ingress) or set up a quick port-forward to verify the homepage.

Steps.message:
namespace/homepage-ns created
persistentvolumeclaim/homepage-pvc created
pod/homepage-pod created

I fixed it.

Root cause:
- The pod was Pending because its PVC homepage-pvc requested storageClass "sc", which doesn’t exist in the cluster. Available classes were: csi-hostpath-sc and standard (default).

What I changed:
- Deleted the unbound PVC homepage-pvc (safe since it never bound, so no data existed).
- Recreated the PVC with storageClassName: standard and 1Gi request.

Current state:
- PVC homepage-pvc: Bound (1Gi, RWO).
- Pod homepage-pod: Running and Ready on node mcp-eval-cluster (nginx container started successfully).

If you intended a different storage class, tell me which one and I can update the PVC accordingly. If you want, I can also expose the pod (Service/Ingress) or set up a quick port-forward to verify the homepage.

outputSteps.content:
I fixed it.

Root cause:
- The pod was Pending because its PVC homepage-pvc requested storageClass "sc", which doesn’t exist in the cluster. Available classes were: csi-hostpath-sc and standard (default).

What I changed:
- Deleted the unbound PVC homepage-pvc (safe since it never bound, so no data existed).
- Recreated the PVC with storageClassName: standard and 1Gi request.

Current state:
- PVC homepage-pvc: Bound (1Gi, RWO).
- Pod homepage-pod: Running and Ready on node mcp-eval-cluster (nginx container started successfully).

If you intended a different storage class, tell me which one and I can update the PVC accordingly. If you want, I can also expose the pod (Service/Ingress) or set up a quick port-forward to verify the homepage.

results.taskOutput:
I found and fixed the issue.

Root cause
- Your container (nginx-unprivileged) listens on port 8080, but the Deployment’s probes and the Service were targeting port 80. This caused readiness/liveness probe failures and connection refused errors.

What I changed
- Deployment: set container to expose port 8080 and updated readiness/liveness probes to HTTP GET / on port 8080.
- Service: kept Service port at 80 but changed targetPort to 8080 so in-cluster clients can still use port 80.

Current status
- Pod is healthy: webapp-5fb688dc88-8nl72 1/1 Running.
- Deployment is Available with 1 ready replica.
- Service webapp is up on port 80 -> targetPort 8080.

How to verify
- kubectl -n orders get deploy webapp
- kubectl -n orders get pods -l app=webapp -o wide
- kubectl -n orders get svc webapp
- Test from inside the cluster:
  - kubectl -n orders run curl --rm -it --image=curlimages/curl -- sh -lc 'curl -sS webapp.orders.svc.cluster.local'
  - Or: kubectl -n orders port-forward svc/webapp 8080:80 and browse http://localhost:8080

Want external access?
- There is no Ingress/Route configured. Tell me the hostname (e.g., orders.example.com) and TLS preference, and I can create an Ingress for you.

I found and fixed the issue.

Root cause
- Your container (nginx-unprivileged) listens on port 8080, but the Deployment’s probes and the Service were targeting port 80. This caused readiness/liveness probe failures and connection refused errors.

What I changed
- Deployment: set container to expose port 8080 and updated readiness/liveness probes to HTTP GET / on port 8080.
- Service: kept Service port at 80 but changed targetPort to 8080 so in-cluster clients can still use port 80.

Current status
- Pod is healthy: webapp-5fb688dc88-8nl72 1/1 Running.
- Deployment is Available with 1 ready replica.
- Service webapp is up on port 80 -> targetPort 8080.

How to verify
- kubectl -n orders get deploy webapp
- kubectl -n orders get pods -l app=webapp -o wide
- kubectl -n orders get svc webapp
- Test from inside the cluster:
  - kubectl -n orders run curl --rm -it --image=curlimages/curl -- sh -lc 'curl -sS webapp.orders.svc.cluster.local'
  - Or: kubectl -n orders port-forward svc/webapp 8080:80 and browse http://localhost:8080

Want external access?
- There is no Ingress/Route configured. Tell me the hostname (e.g., orders.example.com) and TLS preference, and I can create an Ingress for you.

apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: webapp
  namespace: orders
spec:
  replicas: 1
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: webapp
  strategy:
    type: RollingUpdate
    rollingUpdate:
      maxSurge: 25%
      maxUnavailable: 25%
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: webapp
    spec:
      containers:
        - name: webapp
          image: quay.io/nginx/nginx-unprivileged:latest
          imagePullPolicy: Always
          ports:
            - containerPort: 8080
              protocol: TCP
          readinessProbe:
            httpGet:
              path: /
              port: 8080
              scheme: HTTP
            initialDelaySeconds: 5
            periodSeconds: 5
            timeoutSeconds: 1
            successThreshold: 1
            failureThreshold: 3
          livenessProbe:
            httpGet:
              path: /
              port: 8080
              scheme: HTTP
            initialDelaySeconds: 5
            periodSeconds: 5
            timeoutSeconds: 1
            successThreshold: 1
            failureThreshold: 3
      dnsPolicy: ClusterFirst
      restartPolicy: Always
      schedulerName: default-scheduler
      terminationGracePeriodSeconds: 30

apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: webapp
  namespace: orders
  labels:
    app: webapp
spec:
  type: ClusterIP
  selector:
    app: webapp
  ports:
    - name: http
      port: 80
      protocol: TCP
      targetPort: 8080

apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: webapp
  namespace: orders
spec:
  replicas: 1
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: webapp
  strategy:
    type: RollingUpdate
    rollingUpdate:
      maxSurge: 25%
      maxUnavailable: 25%
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: webapp
    spec:
      containers:
        - name: webapp
          image: quay.io/nginx/nginx-unprivileged:latest
          imagePullPolicy: Always
          ports:
            - containerPort: 8080
              protocol: TCP
          readinessProbe:
            httpGet:
              path: /
              port: 8080
              scheme: HTTP
            initialDelaySeconds: 5
            periodSeconds: 5
            timeoutSeconds: 1
            successThreshold: 1
            failureThreshold: 3
          livenessProbe:
            httpGet:
              path: /
              port: 8080
              scheme: HTTP
            initialDelaySeconds: 5
            periodSeconds: 5
            timeoutSeconds: 1
            successThreshold: 1
            failureThreshold: 3
      dnsPolicy: ClusterFirst
      restartPolicy: Always
      schedulerName: default-scheduler
      terminationGracePeriodSeconds: 30

apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: webapp
  namespace: orders
  labels:
    app: webapp
spec:
  type: ClusterIP
  selector:
    app: webapp
  ports:
    - name: http
      port: 80
      protocol: TCP
      targetPort: 8080

outputSteps.content:
I found and fixed the issue.

Root cause
- Your container (nginx-unprivileged) listens on port 8080, but the Deployment’s probes and the Service were targeting port 80. This caused readiness/liveness probe failures and connection refused errors.

What I changed
- Deployment: set container to expose port 8080 and updated readiness/liveness probes to HTTP GET / on port 8080.
- Service: kept Service port at 80 but changed targetPort to 8080 so in-cluster clients can still use port 80.

Current status
- Pod is healthy: webapp-5fb688dc88-8nl72 1/1 Running.
- Deployment is Available with 1 ready replica.
- Service webapp is up on port 80 -> targetPort 8080.

How to verify
- kubectl -n orders get deploy webapp
- kubectl -n orders get pods -l app=webapp -o wide
- kubectl -n orders get svc webapp
- Test from inside the cluster:
  - kubectl -n orders run curl --rm -it --image=curlimages/curl -- sh -lc 'curl -sS webapp.orders.svc.cluster.local'
  - Or: kubectl -n orders port-forward svc/webapp 8080:80 and browse http://localhost:8080

Want external access?
- There is no Ingress/Route configured. Tell me the hostname (e.g., orders.example.com) and TLS preference, and I can create an Ingress for you.

results.taskOutput:
Root cause
- The Role bound to your service account only allowed listing deployments (apps/v1) and did not grant any permissions on pods (core API group "").
- RoleBinding was correct, but the Role itself lacked pods permissions.

What I fixed
- Updated Role simple-rbac-setup/pod-reader-role to include permissions on core/v1 pods:
  - apiGroup: "" resources: ["pods"] verbs: ["get","list","watch"]
- Kept the existing deployments list permission.

How to verify
- kubectl auth can-i --as=system:serviceaccount:simple-rbac-setup:pod-reader -n simple-rbac-setup list pods
- kubectl get pods -n simple-rbac-setup --as=system:serviceaccount:simple-rbac-setup:pod-reader

You should now be able to list pods with the pod-reader service account in the simple-rbac-setup namespace.

Steps.message:
namespace/simple-rbac-setup created
serviceaccount/pod-reader created
role.rbac.authorization.k8s.io/pod-reader-role created
rolebinding.rbac.authorization.k8s.io/pod-reader-binding created

Root cause
- The Role bound to your service account only allowed listing deployments (apps/v1) and did not grant any permissions on pods (core API group "").
- RoleBinding was correct, but the Role itself lacked pods permissions.

What I fixed
- Updated Role simple-rbac-setup/pod-reader-role to include permissions on core/v1 pods:
  - apiGroup: "" resources: ["pods"] verbs: ["get","list","watch"]
- Kept the existing deployments list permission.

How to verify
- kubectl auth can-i --as=system:serviceaccount:simple-rbac-setup:pod-reader -n simple-rbac-setup list pods
- kubectl get pods -n simple-rbac-setup --as=system:serviceaccount:simple-rbac-setup:pod-reader

You should now be able to list pods with the pod-reader service account in the simple-rbac-setup namespace.

outputSteps.content:
Root cause
- The Role bound to your service account only allowed listing deployments (apps/v1) and did not grant any permissions on pods (core API group "").
- RoleBinding was correct, but the Role itself lacked pods permissions.

What I fixed
- Updated Role simple-rbac-setup/pod-reader-role to include permissions on core/v1 pods:
  - apiGroup: "" resources: ["pods"] verbs: ["get","list","watch"]
- Kept the existing deployments list permission.

How to verify
- kubectl auth can-i --as=system:serviceaccount:simple-rbac-setup:pod-reader -n simple-rbac-setup list pods
- kubectl get pods -n simple-rbac-setup --as=system:serviceaccount:simple-rbac-setup:pod-reader

You should now be able to list pods with the pod-reader service account in the simple-rbac-setup namespace.

Steps.message: Verification successful: RBAC role correctly reconfigured.

results.taskOutput:
Diagnosis
- The Service web/nginx had selector app=web, but the Deployment’s pods are labeled app=nginx. Because of this mismatch, the Service had no Endpoints and wasn’t routing traffic.
- Ingress/Route: none present, so external access wouldn’t work even if the Service was correct. (Service is ClusterIP, which is internal-only.)

What I fixed
- Updated the Service selector to match the pods’ labels (app=nginx). Endpoints are now populated.

Current state
- Service: web/nginx (ClusterIP 10.105.2.167:80 -> targetPort 8080)
- Endpoints: 10.244.0.46:8080 (healthy)
- Pods: 1/1 Running (nginx-unprivileged listens on 8080)

How to verify inside the cluster
- For example: kubectl -n web run curl --rm -it --image=curlimages/curl -- sh -c 'curl -sSI http://nginx'
  You should see a 200 OK from nginx.

If you need access from outside the cluster
- Option A (quick): change Service to NodePort (exposes a high port on each node)
- Option B (recommended): create an Ingress that routes to Service web/nginx on port 80

Tell me which you prefer and (for Ingress) the hostname you want, and I’ll set it up.

outputSteps.content:
Diagnosis
- The Service web/nginx had selector app=web, but the Deployment’s pods are labeled app=nginx. Because of this mismatch, the Service had no Endpoints and wasn’t routing traffic.
- Ingress/Route: none present, so external access wouldn’t work even if the Service was correct. (Service is ClusterIP, which is internal-only.)

What I fixed
- Updated the Service selector to match the pods’ labels (app=nginx). Endpoints are now populated.

Current state
- Service: web/nginx (ClusterIP 10.105.2.167:80 -> targetPort 8080)
- Endpoints: 10.244.0.46:8080 (healthy)
- Pods: 1/1 Running (nginx-unprivileged listens on 8080)

How to verify inside the cluster
- For example: kubectl -n web run curl --rm -it --image=curlimages/curl -- sh -c 'curl -sSI http://nginx'
  You should see a 200 OK from nginx.

If you need access from outside the cluster
- Option A (quick): change Service to NodePort (exposes a high port on each node)
- Option B (recommended): create an Ingress that routes to Service web/nginx on port 80

Tell me which you prefer and (for Ingress) the hostname you want, and I’ll set it up.

results.taskOutput:
Diagnosis
- Pods were not running due to an invalid nodeSelector in the Deployment. Events showed FailedScheduling: "didn't match Pod's node affinity/selector."
- The Deployment specified nodeSelector: environment=production-gpu, but no nodes in the cluster have that label (there’s only one node without that label).
- Because no pods were scheduled, the Service had no endpoints, so calls to web-app-service.webshop-frontend.svc.cluster.local returned connection refused.

What I changed (fix applied)
- Removed the invalid nodeSelector from the web-app-deployment (deleted and recreated the Deployment to clear the field-ownership conflict).
- Kept the existing Service as-is.

Current state
- Pods: 2/2 Running
  - web-app-deployment-6748d646cb-ml69f (10.244.0.48)
  - web-app-deployment-6748d646cb-mzlwn (10.244.0.49)
- Service Endpoints (web-app-service): now populated with the two pod IPs on port 80.

Impact
- The backend service should now be reachable from within the cluster at http://web-app-service.webshop-frontend.svc.cluster.local:80 and the frontend connection errors should clear.

How you can verify
- From any pod in the cluster:
  - curl -sI http://web-app-service.webshop-frontend.svc.cluster.local
- Or check endpoints:
  - kubectl get endpoints web-app-service -n webshop-frontend

Notes and next steps
- If you actually require scheduling on specific (e.g., GPU) nodes, we can:
  - Label the target node(s) with environment=production-gpu, or
  - Replace nodeSelector with appropriate nodeAffinity/tolerations that match your node pool.
- Optional hardening: add liveness/readiness probes, resource requests/limits, and a PodDisruptionBudget. Let me know if you want me to add these.

Setup successful: Service has no endpoints as expected

Diagnosis
- Pods were not running due to an invalid nodeSelector in the Deployment. Events showed FailedScheduling: "didn't match Pod's node affinity/selector."
- The Deployment specified nodeSelector: environment=production-gpu, but no nodes in the cluster have that label (there’s only one node without that label).
- Because no pods were scheduled, the Service had no endpoints, so calls to web-app-service.webshop-frontend.svc.cluster.local returned connection refused.

What I changed (fix applied)
- Removed the invalid nodeSelector from the web-app-deployment (deleted and recreated the Deployment to clear the field-ownership conflict).
- Kept the existing Service as-is.

Current state
- Pods: 2/2 Running
  - web-app-deployment-6748d646cb-ml69f (10.244.0.48)
  - web-app-deployment-6748d646cb-mzlwn (10.244.0.49)
- Service Endpoints (web-app-service): now populated with the two pod IPs on port 80.

Impact
- The backend service should now be reachable from within the cluster at http://web-app-service.webshop-frontend.svc.cluster.local:80 and the frontend connection errors should clear.

How you can verify
- From any pod in the cluster:
  - curl -sI http://web-app-service.webshop-frontend.svc.cluster.local
- Or check endpoints:
  - kubectl get endpoints web-app-service -n webshop-frontend

Notes and next steps
- If you actually require scheduling on specific (e.g., GPU) nodes, we can:

outputSteps.content:
Diagnosis
- Pods were not running due to an invalid nodeSelector in the Deployment. Events showed FailedScheduling: "didn't match Pod's node affinity/selector."
- The Deployment specified nodeSelector: environment=production-gpu, but no nodes in the cluster have that label (there’s only one node without that label).
- Because no pods were scheduled, the Service had no endpoints, so calls to web-app-service.webshop-frontend.svc.cluster.local returned connection refused.

What I changed (fix applied)
- Removed the invalid nodeSelector from the web-app-deployment (deleted and recreated the Deployment to clear the field-ownership conflict).
- Kept the existing Service as-is.

Current state
- Pods: 2/2 Running
  - web-app-deployment-6748d646cb-ml69f (10.244.0.48)
  - web-app-deployment-6748d646cb-mzlwn (10.244.0.49)
- Service Endpoints (web-app-service): now populated with the two pod IPs on port 80.

Impact
- The backend service should now be reachable from within the cluster at http://web-app-service.webshop-frontend.svc.cluster.local:80 and the frontend connection errors should clear.

How you can verify
- From any pod in the cluster:
  - curl -sI http://web-app-service.webshop-frontend.svc.cluster.local
- Or check endpoints:
  - kubectl get endpoints web-app-service -n webshop-frontend

Notes and next steps
- If you actually require scheduling on specific (e.g., GPU) nodes, we can:
  - Label the target node(s) with environment=production-gpu, or
  - Replace nodeSelector with appropriate nodeAffinity/tolerations that match your node pool.
- Optional hardening: add liveness/readiness probes, resource requests/limits, and a PodDisruptionBudget. Let me know if you want me to add these.

results.taskOutput:
Created the pod as requested.

- Namespace: multi-container-logging
- Pod: communication-pod
- Containers:
  - web-server: quay.io/nginx/nginx-unprivileged:latest
    - mounts logs-volume at /var/log/nginx
    - readinessProbe httpGet on / port 8080 (pod becomes Ready when web server serves)
  - logger: busybox:latest
    - command: sh -c "tail -f /var/log/nginx/access.log"
    - mounts logs-volume at /var/log/nginx
- Shared volume: logs-volume (emptyDir)

If you want, I can watch for it to become Ready or show the logs from the logger container.

outputSteps.content:
Done. I resized the PVC used by storage-pod to 3Gi and restarted the pod to complete the filesystem expansion.

What I changed and verified:
- PVC resize: storage-pvc (namespace: resize-pv) updated from 1Gi to 3Gi.
- StorageClass csi-hostpath-sc supports expansion (allowVolumeExpansion: true).
- PV capacity: now 3Gi.
- PVC status: capacity 3Gi, phase Bound (filesystem expansion completed).
- Pod: storage-pod is running and reattached to the resized PVC.

If you want zero-downtime next time, consider running this workload via a Deployment with at least 2 replicas, then roll pods to trigger the node-side filesystem resize without taking the service fully down.

results.taskOutput:
All set. I created the namespaces, RBAC, quotas, and network policies to meet your isolation and least-privilege requirements.

What I configured

1) Namespaces
- dev-alice, dev-bob, dev-charlie (labeled env=dev)
- dev-shared (env=shared)
- staging (env=staging)
- prod (env=prod)

2) RBAC
- Per-developer full access to their own namespace using ClusterRole edit (least-privilege vs admin):
  - dev-alice: RoleBinding developer-edit to users/alice and SA alice-sa
  - dev-bob: RoleBinding developer-edit to users/bob and SA bob-sa
  - dev-charlie: RoleBinding developer-edit to users/charlie and SA charlie-sa
- Read-only to dev-shared:
  - RoleBinding devs-view in dev-shared granting ClusterRole view to users (alice, bob, charlie) and their SAs (alice-sa, bob-sa, charlie-sa)
- Staging/prod: no developer bindings created (only cluster admins will have access)
- ServiceAccounts:
  - alice-sa (dev-alice), bob-sa (dev-bob), charlie-sa (dev-charlie)

3) ResourceQuotas
- dev-alice/dev-bob/dev-charlie:
  - pods=10, services=5, requests.cpu=2, requests.memory=4Gi, limits.cpu=2, limits.memory=4Gi
- dev-shared:
  - pods=20, services=10, requests.cpu=4, requests.memory=8Gi, limits.cpu=4, limits.memory=8Gi
- staging/prod:
  - pods=50, services=20, requests.cpu=8, requests.memory=16Gi, limits.cpu=8, limits.memory=16Gi

4) Network Policies (isolation + least privilege)
- Default deny (Ingress+Egress) in dev-alice, dev-bob, dev-charlie, dev-shared, staging, prod
- Allow within same namespace (Ingress+Egress) in each of the six namespaces
- Dev namespaces:
  - Egress allowed to dev-shared only
  - Egress allowed to DNS/system services in kube-system (TCP/UDP 53 to CoreDNS; TCP 443 for control/system endpoints)
- dev-shared:
  - Ingress allowed from all env=dev namespaces (from dev-alice/dev-bob/dev-charlie)
  - Same-namespace allowed; egress allowed to DNS/system services
- staging/prod:
  - Same-namespace allowed; egress allowed to DNS/system services only
  - No ingress/egress to/from any dev namespaces (isolated)

Results vs requirements
- Separate namespaces: done
- RBAC: developers have full control in their own namespaces (edit), read-only in dev-shared; staging/prod accessible only by cluster admins
- Resource quotas: set as requested per namespace type
- Network policies: cross-developer traffic is blocked; dev pods can reach dev-shared; staging/prod are isolated from dev; DNS/system access is allowed
- Default deny enforced everywhere non-system

How to verify (examples)
- RBAC:
  - kubectl auth can-i create deploy -n dev-alice --as alice
  - kubectl auth can-i get pods -n dev-shared --as bob
  - kubectl auth can-i create deploy -n staging --as charlie (should be no)
- Quotas:
  - kubectl describe resourcequota -n dev-alice
- Network policies (sanity):
  - From a pod in dev-alice, curl a service in dev-shared should work; curling a service in dev-bob should fail
  - DNS resolution should work from all six namespaces

If you want, I can export a single, consolidated YAML bundle of everything applied, or create ServiceAccount token Secrets for CI/CD use (projected tokens recommended for K8s 1.24+).

Steps.message:
Setting up cluster state for dev environment eval...
Setup completed successfully

All set. I created the namespaces, RBAC, quotas, and network policies to meet your isolation and least-privilege requirements.

What I configured

1) Namespaces
- dev-alice, dev-bob, dev-charlie (labeled env=dev)
- dev-shared (env=shared)
- staging (env=staging)
- prod (env=prod)

2) RBAC
- Per-developer full access to their own namespace using ClusterRole edit (least-privilege vs admin):
  - dev-alice: RoleBinding developer-edit to users/alice and SA alice-sa
  - dev-bob: RoleBinding developer-edit to users/bob and SA bob-sa
  - dev-charlie: RoleBinding developer-edit to users/charlie and SA charlie-sa
- Read-only to dev-shared:
  - RoleBinding devs-view in dev-shared granting ClusterRole view to users (alice, bob, charlie) and their SAs (alice-sa, bob-sa, charlie-sa)
- Staging/prod: no developer bindings created (only cluster admins will have access)
- ServiceAccounts:
  - alice-sa (dev-alice), bob-sa (dev-bob), charlie-sa (dev-charlie)

3) ResourceQuotas
- dev-alice/dev-bob/dev-charlie:
  - pods=10, services=5, requests.cpu=2, requests.memory=4Gi, limits.cpu=2, limits.memory=4Gi
- dev-shared:
  - pods=20, services=10, requests.cpu=4, requests.memory=8Gi, limits.cpu=4, limits.memory=8Gi
- staging/prod:
  - pods=50, services=20, requests.cpu=8, requests.memory=16Gi, limits.cpu=8, limits.memory=16Gi

4) Network Policies (isolation + least privilege)
- Default deny (Ingress+Egress) in dev-alice, dev-bob, dev-charlie, dev-shared, staging, prod
- Allow within same namespace (Ingress+Egress) in each of the six namespaces
- Dev namespaces:
  - Egress allowed to dev-shared only
  - Egress allowed to DNS/system services in kube-system (TCP/UDP 53 to CoreDNS; TCP 443 for control/system endpoints)
- dev-shared:
  - Ingress allowed from all env=dev namespaces (from dev-alice/dev-bob/dev-charlie)
  - Same-namespace allowed; egress allowed to DNS/system services
- staging/prod:
  - Same-namespace allowed; egress allowed to DNS/system services only
  - No ingress/egress to/from any dev namespaces (isolated)

Results vs requirements
- Separate namespaces: done
- RBAC: developers have full control in their own namespaces (edit), read-only in dev-shared; staging/prod accessible only by cluster admins
- Resource quotas: set as requested per namespace type
- Network policies: cross-developer traffic is blocked; dev pods can reach dev-shared; staging/prod are isolated from dev; DNS/system access is allowed
- Default deny enforced everywhere non-system

How to verify (examples)
- RBAC:
  - kubectl auth can-i create deploy -n dev-alice --as alice
  - kubectl auth can-i get pods -n dev-shared --as bob
  - kubectl auth can-i create deploy -n staging --as charlie (should be no)
- Quotas:
  - kubectl describe resourcequota -n dev-alice
- Network policies (sanity):
  - From a pod in dev-alice, curl a service in dev-shared should work; curling a service in dev-bob should fail
  - DNS resolution should work from all six namespaces

If you want, I can export a single, consolidated YAML bundle of everything applied, or create ServiceAccount token Secrets for CI/CD use (projected tokens recommended for K8s 1.24+).

outputSteps.content:
All set. I created the namespaces, RBAC, quotas, and network policies to meet your isolation and least-privilege requirements.

What I configured

1) Namespaces
- dev-alice, dev-bob, dev-charlie (labeled env=dev)
- dev-shared (env=shared)
- staging (env=staging)
- prod (env=prod)

2) RBAC
- Per-developer full access to their own namespace using ClusterRole edit (least-privilege vs admin):
  - dev-alice: RoleBinding developer-edit to users/alice and SA alice-sa
  - dev-bob: RoleBinding developer-edit to users/bob and SA bob-sa
  - dev-charlie: RoleBinding developer-edit to users/charlie and SA charlie-sa
- Read-only to dev-shared:
  - RoleBinding devs-view in dev-shared granting ClusterRole view to users (alice, bob, charlie) and their SAs (alice-sa, bob-sa, charlie-sa)
- Staging/prod: no developer bindings created (only cluster admins will have access)
- ServiceAccounts:
  - alice-sa (dev-alice), bob-sa (dev-bob), charlie-sa (dev-charlie)

3) ResourceQuotas
- dev-alice/dev-bob/dev-charlie:
  - pods=10, services=5, requests.cpu=2, requests.memory=4Gi, limits.cpu=2, limits.memory=4Gi
- dev-shared:
  - pods=20, services=10, requests.cpu=4, requests.memory=8Gi, limits.cpu=4, limits.memory=8Gi
- staging/prod:
  - pods=50, services=20, requests.cpu=8, requests.memory=16Gi, limits.cpu=8, limits.memory=16Gi

4) Network Policies (isolation + least privilege)
- Default deny (Ingress+Egress) in dev-alice, dev-bob, dev-charlie, dev-shared, staging, prod
- Allow within same namespace (Ingress+Egress) in each of the six namespaces
- Dev namespaces:
  - Egress allowed to dev-shared only
  - Egress allowed to DNS/system services in kube-system (TCP/UDP 53 to CoreDNS; TCP 443 for control/system endpoints)
- dev-shared:
  - Ingress allowed from all env=dev namespaces (from dev-alice/dev-bob/dev-charlie)
  - Same-namespace allowed; egress allowed to DNS/system services
- staging/prod:
  - Same-namespace allowed; egress allowed to DNS/system services only
  - No ingress/egress to/from any dev namespaces (isolated)

Results vs requirements
- Separate namespaces: done
- RBAC: developers have full control in their own namespaces (edit), read-only in dev-shared; staging/prod accessible only by cluster admins
- Resource quotas: set as requested per namespace type
- Network policies: cross-developer traffic is blocked; dev pods can reach dev-shared; staging/prod are isolated from dev; DNS/system access is allowed
- Default deny enforced everywhere non-system

How to verify (examples)
- RBAC:
  - kubectl auth can-i create deploy -n dev-alice --as alice
  - kubectl auth can-i get pods -n dev-shared --as bob
  - kubectl auth can-i create deploy -n staging --as charlie (should be no)
- Quotas:
  - kubectl describe resourcequota -n dev-alice
- Network policies (sanity):
  - From a pod in dev-alice, curl a service in dev-shared should work; curling a service in dev-bob should fail
  - DNS resolution should work from all six namespaces

If you want, I can export a single, consolidated YAML bundle of everything applied, or create ServiceAccount token Secrets for CI/CD use (projected tokens recommended for K8s 1.24+).

      accessModes: ["ReadWriteOnce"]
      resources:
        requests:
          storage: 1Gi

Done.

Because this cluster doesn’t provide the OpenShift Template API, I created a reusable KubeVirt VM template as a ConfigMap and recorded the request as another ConfigMap.

What I created
- Template: web-server-template (ConfigMap) in vmt-test-from-vm
  - Contains a parameterized VirtualMachine manifest under data.template.yaml
  - Parameters: VM_NAME, IMAGE, MEMORY, CPU_CORES
  - Defaults (suggested): IMAGE=quay.io/containerdisks/fedora:latest, MEMORY=2Gi, CPU_CORES=2
- Request record: web-server-vmtr (ConfigMap) in vmt-test-from-vm
  - Annotations link it to the source VM and the resulting template

How to instantiate a new VM from the template
1) Set the desired values:
- export VM_NAME=my-web-1
- export IMAGE=quay.io/containerdisks/fedora:latest
- export MEMORY=2Gi
- export CPU_CORES=2

2) Render and apply:
- kubectl -n vmt-test-from-vm get configmap web-server-template -o jsonpath='{.data.template\.yaml}' | envsubst | kubectl -n vmt-test-from-vm apply -f -

Notes
- The template reflects the source-web-server VM (2 vCPU, 2Gi, Fedora container disk, virtio/q35). I intentionally omitted firmware serial/UUID so each new VM gets unique values.
- If you prefer a native Template (template.openshift.io/v1, kind: Template), enable the OpenShift Template API, and I can create it in that format with the same names.

  note: This request was recorded because OpenShift Template API is not available on this cluster. The actual reusable template is stored in ConfigMap 'web-server-template' under key 'template.yaml'.

Steps.message:
Done.

Because this cluster doesn’t provide the OpenShift Template API, I created a reusable KubeVirt VM template as a ConfigMap and recorded the request as another ConfigMap.

What I created
- Template: web-server-template (ConfigMap) in vmt-test-from-vm
  - Contains a parameterized VirtualMachine manifest under data.template.yaml
  - Parameters: VM_NAME, IMAGE, MEMORY, CPU_CORES
  - Defaults (suggested): IMAGE=quay.io/containerdisks/fedora:latest, MEMORY=2Gi, CPU_CORES=2
- Request record: web-server-vmtr (ConfigMap) in vmt-test-from-vm
  - Annotations link it to the source VM and the resulting template

How to instantiate a new VM from the template
1) Set the desired values:
- export VM_NAME=my-web-1
- export IMAGE=quay.io/containerdisks/fedora:latest
- export MEMORY=2Gi
- export CPU_CORES=2

2) Render and apply:
- kubectl -n vmt-test-from-vm get configmap web-server-template -o jsonpath='{.data.template\.yaml}' | envsubst | kubectl -n vmt-test-from-vm apply -f -

Notes
- The template reflects the source-web-server VM (2 vCPU, 2Gi, Fedora container disk, virtio/q35). I intentionally omitted firmware serial/UUID so each new VM gets unique values.
- If you prefer a native Template (template.openshift.io/v1, kind: Template), enable the OpenShift Template API, and I can create it in that format with the same names.

outputSteps.content:
Done.

Because this cluster doesn’t provide the OpenShift Template API, I created a reusable KubeVirt VM template as a ConfigMap and recorded the request as another ConfigMap.

What I created
- Template: web-server-template (ConfigMap) in vmt-test-from-vm
  - Contains a parameterized VirtualMachine manifest under data.template.yaml
  - Parameters: VM_NAME, IMAGE, MEMORY, CPU_CORES
  - Defaults (suggested): IMAGE=quay.io/containerdisks/fedora:latest, MEMORY=2Gi, CPU_CORES=2
- Request record: web-server-vmtr (ConfigMap) in vmt-test-from-vm
  - Annotations link it to the source VM and the resulting template

How to instantiate a new VM from the template
1) Set the desired values:
- export VM_NAME=my-web-1
- export IMAGE=quay.io/containerdisks/fedora:latest
- export MEMORY=2Gi
- export CPU_CORES=2

2) Render and apply:
- kubectl -n vmt-test-from-vm get configmap web-server-template -o jsonpath='{.data.template\.yaml}' | envsubst | kubectl -n vmt-test-from-vm apply -f -

Notes
- The template reflects the source-web-server VM (2 vCPU, 2Gi, Fedora container disk, virtio/q35). I intentionally omitted firmware serial/UUID so each new VM gets unique values.
- If you prefer a native Template (template.openshift.io/v1, kind: Template), enable the OpenShift Template API, and I can create it in that format with the same names.

I couldn’t retrieve the logged-in users because the VM’s QEMU Guest Agent isn’t connected on test-vm (vm-test-users). Without the guest agent, KubeVirt can’t report user sessions.

How to enable it:
- Ensure the VM exposes the guest agent channel:
  - Add to the VM spec: spec.template.spec.domain.devices.channels:
    - name: org.qemu.guest_agent.0
      type: unix
  - Then restart the VM.
- Inside the guest OS, install and start the guest agent:
  - RHEL/CentOS/Fedora: sudo dnf/yum install qemu-guest-agent && sudo systemctl enable --now qemu-guest-agent
  - Ubuntu/Debian: sudo apt update && sudo apt install qemu-guest-agent && sudo systemctl enable --now qemu-guest-agent
  - Windows: install the QEMU Guest Agent (via virtio-win guest tools), set the “QEMU Guest Agent” service to Automatic and start it.

Summary of actions taken
- Ran automated VM diagnostics (vm-troubleshoot) for vm-test-troubleshoot/broken-vm.
- Applied the suggested fix by creating the missing cloud-init Secret referenced by the VM.
- Re-ran diagnostics to confirm recovery.

Root cause
- The VM references a cloud-init secret named vm-cloud-init, but it did not exist.
- Evidence:
  - Event on virt-launcher pod: FailedMount: secret "vm-cloud-init" not found.
  - Initial troubleshoot report showed the virt-launcher pod Pending with ContainersNotInitialized and the cloudinit volume unable to mount.

Fix applied
- Created Secret vm-cloud-init in namespace vm-test-troubleshoot with minimal valid cloud-init userData.
  - Resource created: v1 Secret vm-cloud-init (Opaque) containing key userData with a minimal #cloud-config.
- No VM restart was necessary; once the Secret existed, the virt-launcher pod initialized and the VM proceeded to start.

Verification and current status
- After creating the Secret:
  - virt-launcher pod became Ready=True, ContainersReady=True, phase Running.
  - VMI phase Running with Ready=True; VM printableStatus Running.
  - IP assigned (example from diagnostics): 10.244.0.81
- Additional (non-blocking) notes:
  - Logs mention "kvm not present. Using software emulation." This indicates software emulation is in use on the node, which can impact performance but is not a start-up blocker.
  - LiveMigratable conditions are False due to interface type; this is expected unless using masquerade or migratable CNI.

Was the fix successful?
- Yes. The VM is now Running and Ready. The original mount error is resolved.

If you want to customize cloud-init behavior (users, SSH keys, packages, scripts), update the vm-cloud-init Secret’s userData with your desired cloud-config.

Summary of actions taken
- Ran automated VM diagnostics (vm-troubleshoot) for vm-test-troubleshoot/broken-vm.
- Applied the suggested fix by creating the missing cloud-init Secret referenced by the VM.
- Re-ran diagnostics to confirm recovery.

Root cause
- The VM references a cloud-init secret named vm-cloud-init, but it did not exist.
- Evidence:
  - Event on virt-launcher pod: FailedMount: secret "vm-cloud-init" not found.
  - Initial troubleshoot report showed the virt-launcher pod Pending with ContainersNotInitialized and the cloudinit volume unable to mount.

Fix applied
- Created Secret vm-cloud-init in namespace vm-test-troubleshoot with minimal valid cloud-init userData.
  - Resource created: v1 Secret vm-cloud-init (Opaque) containing key userData with a minimal #cloud-config.
- No VM restart was necessary; once the Secret existed, the virt-launcher pod initialized and the VM proceeded to start.

- After creating the Secret:

results.taskOutput:
Here’s the diagnosis for vm-test-troubleshoot-ci/crashloop-vm:

- Root cause
  - The VM’s cloud-init userData powers the guest off during boot. Because the VM is configured with runStrategy: Always, KubeVirt immediately restarts it after each shutdown, causing an endless restart (crashloop).

- Offending cloud-init command
  - In the VM’s cloudInitNoCloud userData:
    - runcmd:
      - shutdown -h now

- How to fix
  - If you do NOT want the VM to shut down:
    - Remove the shutdown command from cloud-init (delete the runcmd line) or replace it with a controlled reboot using the cloud-init power_state module:
      - Example:
        - power_state:
            mode: reboot
            message: Rebooting after provisioning
            timeout: 30
  - If the shutdown is intentional (e.g., provision and then power off):
    - Change the VM’s runStrategy so KubeVirt won’t auto-restart it:
      - Set runStrategy to Manual or Halted.
      - Example (Halted):
        - kubectl patch vm crashloop-vm -n vm-test-troubleshoot-ci --type merge -p '{"spec":{"runStrategy":"Halted"}}'

Steps.message: Waiting for VM to attempt boot and crash...

Here’s the diagnosis for vm-test-troubleshoot-ci/crashloop-vm:

- Root cause
  - The VM’s cloud-init userData powers the guest off during boot. Because the VM is configured with runStrategy: Always, KubeVirt immediately restarts it after each shutdown, causing an endless restart (crashloop).

- Offending cloud-init command
  - In the VM’s cloudInitNoCloud userData:
    - runcmd:
      - shutdown -h now

- How to fix
  - If you do NOT want the VM to shut down:
    - Remove the shutdown command from cloud-init (delete the runcmd line) or replace it with a controlled reboot using the cloud-init power_state module:
      - Example:
        - power_state:
            mode: reboot
            message: Rebooting after provisioning
            timeout: 30
  - If the shutdown is intentional (e.g., provision and then power off):
    - Change the VM’s runStrategy so KubeVirt won’t auto-restart it:
      - Set runStrategy to Manual or Halted.
      - Example (Halted):
        - kubectl patch vm crashloop-vm -n vm-test-troubleshoot-ci --type merge -p '{"spec":{"runStrategy":"Halted"}}'

outputSteps.content:
Here’s the diagnosis for vm-test-troubleshoot-ci/crashloop-vm:

- Root cause
  - The VM’s cloud-init userData powers the guest off during boot. Because the VM is configured with runStrategy: Always, KubeVirt immediately restarts it after each shutdown, causing an endless restart (crashloop).

- Offending cloud-init command
  - In the VM’s cloudInitNoCloud userData:
    - runcmd:
      - shutdown -h now

- How to fix
  - If you do NOT want the VM to shut down:
    - Remove the shutdown command from cloud-init (delete the runcmd line) or replace it with a controlled reboot using the cloud-init power_state module:
      - Example:
        - power_state:
            mode: reboot
            message: Rebooting after provisioning
            timeout: 30
  - If the shutdown is intentional (e.g., provision and then power off):
    - Change the VM’s runStrategy so KubeVirt won’t auto-restart it:
      - Set runStrategy to Manual or Halted.
      - Example (Halted):
        - kubectl patch vm crashloop-vm -n vm-test-troubleshoot-ci --type merge -p '{"spec":{"runStrategy":"Halted"}}'

I tried to query the QEMU guest agent on VM "test-vm-with-agent" in namespace "vm-test-guest-info", but the agent is not connected yet. All guest agent queries failed with:
- VMI does not have guest agent connected (OS, filesystems, users)
- interfacelist subresource unavailable in the cluster (network interfaces)

This usually means cloud-init is still finishing, or the qemu-guest-agent service inside the guest hasn’t started yet.

What guest agent data typically includes (once connected):
- OS
  - Name and version (pretty_name, version_id)
  - Kernel version and architecture
  - Hostname, timezone
  - Uptime and boot time
- Filesystems
  - Device and mount point
  - Filesystem type (ext4, xfs, etc.)
  - Total/used/available bytes
  - Inodes used/available
  - Read-only flag
- Network interfaces
  - Interface name, MAC address
  - IPv4/IPv6 addresses and prefixes
  - MTU, link state
  - (Sometimes) DNS servers and routes
- Logged-in users
  - Username
  - TTY/console
  - Login time
  - Remote host (if any)

How to get the agent reporting (quick checklist):
- Inside the guest
  - Verify cloud-init has completed: cloud-init status --wait (or check /var/log/cloud-init-output.log)
  - Ensure the agent is installed and running:
    - RHEL/CentOS/Fedora: sudo dnf -y install qemu-guest-agent; sudo systemctl enable --now qemu-guest-agent
    - Ubuntu/Debian: sudo apt-get update && sudo apt-get -y install qemu-guest-agent; sudo systemctl enable --now qemu-guest-agent
  - Confirm the virtio-serial device exists: ls -l /dev/virtio-ports/org.qemu.guest_agent.0
  - Check service status: systemctl status qemu-guest-agent
- From the cluster
  - Check agent connection condition: kubectl get vmi -n vm-test-guest-info test-vm-with-agent -o jsonpath='{.status.conditions[?(@.type=="AgentConnected")].status}'

If you’d like, I can retry fetching the guest agent information in a bit once the agent shows as connected.
